title: Paediatric Seizure
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Seizures are transient disturbances of brain function causing abnormal movements, behaviour or consciousness. In low‑resource settings the focus is rapid assessment, identifying reversible causes and stabilising the child.

sections.p: A seizure is a sudden, stereotyped change in behaviour, movement or consciousness caused by abnormal neuronal firing. Diagnosis is clinical; EEG confirms if available.
b: Brief, unprovoked seizure lasting <5 min = epileptic seizure
Provoked seizure: metabolic, infection, toxin, fever

sections.p: Use the WHO seizure severity scale: mild (no loss of consciousness), moderate (brief loss of consciousness, post‑ictal confusion <30 min), severe (status epilepticus or prolonged post‑ictal state).
b: Status epilepticus: seizure >5 min or recurrent seizures without full recovery
Emergency if airway compromise, hypoxia or prolonged convulsion

sections.p: In East African children the commonest precipitants are febrile illness, malaria, meningitis, severe malnutrition and electrolyte disturbances.
b: Infection: cerebral malaria, bacterial meningitis, HIV encephalitis
Metabolic: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia
Fever: febrile seizures (age 6 mo‑5 yr, usually benign)
Structural: neurocysticercosis, tuberculoma, trauma
Toxins: herbal remedies, organophosphates, antimalarial overdose

sections.p: Typical presentations include generalized tonic‑clonic activity, focal jerks, or subtle automatisms. Ask about trigger, duration, recovery, and preceding illness.
b: Generalised tonic‑clonic: loss of consciousness, stiffening then rhythmic jerks
Focal: unilateral jerking, eye deviation, may evolve to generalised
Febrile: occurs within 24 h of fever, <15 min, no prior epilepsy

t.b: Is hypoglycaemia the trigger? <2.5 mmol/L confirms need for dextrose

t.a: Full blood count & malaria rapid test
t.b: Detect infection or malaria; positive malaria → treat urgently
Identify metabolic precipitants; hyponatraemia <130 mmol/L or calcium <2.0 mmol/L
Confirms bacterial/fungal infection; CSF pleocytosis, low glucose
Distinguishes epileptic from non‑epileptic events; abnormal spikes support epilepsy

t.a: Neuro‑imaging (CT/MRI) – if focal signs or trauma
t.b: Detect structural lesions; if unavailable, manage clinically

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent care and recognise sequelae.
b: Status epilepticus, respiratory compromise, severe hypoglycaemia
Post‑ictal apnea, aspiration, traumatic injury
Recurrent seizures causing neuro‑cognitive decline

sections.p: Stabilise airway, treat reversible causes, then give antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) if seizure persists.
b: Airway & breathing: position child laterally, give oxygen if SpO₂ <90 %
Correct hypoglycaemia: IV dextrose 10 % bolus
Treat malaria or meningitis promptly according to national guidelines
Second‑line: phenobarbital if seizure continues
Avoid drugs that lower seizure threshold (e.g., bupropion, high‑dose quinine)
Monitor vitals, glucose, and seizure frequency

sections.p: Arrange outpatient review to assess epilepsy risk, optimise nutrition and immunisations, and educate caregivers.
b: If first febrile seizure and normal exam, no long‑term AED needed
For recurrent seizures, start maintenance AED (phenobarbital or carbamazepine) after acute phase
Educate on fever control, malaria prophylaxis, safe herbal use

sections.p: Conditions that mimic seizures must be considered.
b: Syncope with convulsive movements – brief loss of consciousness, rapid recovery
Psychogenic non‑epileptic seizures – prolonged, variable movements, no post‑ictal confusion
Tonic dystonia from drug toxicity – sustained posture, not rhythmic

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading investigations.
b: Normal glucose after delayed measurement may miss transient hypoglycaemia
Rapid malaria test can be false‑negative early; consider microscopy if suspicion high
EEG may be normal after a single seizure; repeat if epilepsy suspected

whenToSeekHelp: Seizure lasting >5 min or recurrent without recovery
Airway obstruction, cyanosis, or inability to protect airway
Signs of severe infection (high fever, neck stiffness, altered consciousness)

faq.q: What is the first step in a child with a new seizure?
faq.a: Secure airway, breathing and circulation, then check blood glucose.

faq.q: When is a febrile seizure considered an emergency?
faq.a: If it lasts >5 min, recurs, or the child has focal features or impaired recovery.

faq.q: Why avoid bupropion in a child with seizures?
faq.a: It lowers the seizure threshold and can precipitate convulsions.

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with a 2‑minute generalized tonic‑clonic seizure and fever 38.5 °C – what immediate investigations and why? — Check glucose, malaria test, and consider LP if meningitis signs; each rules out common reversible causes.

A child in a malaria‑endemic area has status epilepticus – which drug is first‑line and what monitoring is required? — Give IV/IM diazepam; monitor respiration, oxygen saturation, and treat underlying malaria.

How would you differentiate a febrile seizure from an acute symptomatic seizure due to meningitis? — Fever alone, age 6 mo‑5 yr, short duration, normal exam favour febrile; neck stiffness, altered consciousness, abnormal CSF suggest meningitis.

A child with repeated focal seizures after a head injury – what imaging is indicated and why? — CT scan (or MRI if available) to look for intracranial bleed or contusion that may need neurosurgical referral.

Why is phenobarbital preferred over carbamazepine for acute seizure control in low‑resource settings? — It is inexpensive, available orally or IV, and has a long half‑life; carbamazepine requires titration and monitoring.
What red‑flag features in a seizure history would prompt urgent referral? — Status epilepticus, respiratory compromise, post‑ictal coma, focal neurological deficit, or signs of systemic infection.
Explain why a normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy in a child with a single seizure. — EEG captures only a brief window; interictal spikes may be absent, especially after a first event.

What are the key components of caregiver education after a first febrile seizure? — Fever control, when to seek help, safe sleeping position, and reassurance that long‑term medication is usually unnecessary.
